title: CoRe-WM: Conditioned Response-State World Modeling for Longitudinal Treatment-Response Prediction in Breast DCE-MRI
authors: Lin Zhao, Bowen Chen, Qiaohui Gao, Shaowen Wan, Xiang Li, Wei Liu
abstract: Pathologic complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant chemotherapy is a key prognostic indicator in aggressive breast cancer, yet existing prediction approaches either rely on pretreatment imaging alone, missing the patient's evolving response, or optimize multi-visit classifiers under direct outcome supervision, coupling representation learning with the clinical endpoint. We formulate longitudinal pCR prediction as a world-modeling problem and propose Conditioned Response-state World Modeling (CoRe-WM), which learns a latent state-transition model that predicts the next imaging state from the observed sequence. The transition function is conditioned on patient clinical profile and assigned therapy through additive shift and feature-wise modulation, enabling patient- and treatment-specific dynamics. A Factorized Response State pathway further decouples treatment-response dynamics from imaging appearance by encoding the structural prior that response manifests primarily in lesion morphology. After pretraining, all parameters are frozen and a linear readout predicts pCR at each clinical decision point. We evaluate CoRe-WM on I-SPY2 under five-fold cross-validation and assess cross-cohort transfer on I-SPY1. CoRe-WM achieves the highest discrimination among all evaluated methods at every prospective decision point, and demonstrates robust cross-cohort transfer. Ablation studies identify patient-profile conditioning and the factorized response pathway as the principal contributors. These results establish world-model-based representation learning as a promising framework for outcome prediction in oncology and beyond.

infographic.key_insight: CoRe-WM learns how breast MRI response states evolve during treatment, then uses frozen representations to predict pathologic complete response (pCR).
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support research into treatment-response assessment during neoadjuvant chemotherapy, rather than relying on pretreatment imaging alone.
method: Predicts the next latent imaging state from longitudinal breast DCE-MRI.
Conditions state transitions on patient clinical profiles and assigned therapy, with a separate lesion-morphology response pathway.
Freezes pretrained model parameters and trains a linear pCR readout at each decision point.
infographic.evidence_signal: In five-fold cross-validation on I-SPY2, CoRe-WM reportedly achieved the highest discrimination among evaluated methods at every prospective decision point and showed cross-cohort transfer to I-SPY1.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical performance estimates or prospective clinical validation; this is treatment-response prediction research, not drug discovery or evidence for changing treatment.
infographic.paper_title: CoRe-WM: Conditioned Response-State World Modeling for Longitudinal Treatment-Response Prediction in Breast DCE-MRI

title: Generative Retrieval for Reverse Target Fishing with a Proteome-Scale Benchmark
authors: Zhichao Deng, Haichuan Tan, Xin Hong, Huaizhi Wang, Tao Huang, Bowen Gao
abstract: Reverse target fishing identifies protein targets for a query molecule and is central to drug discovery and repurposing. Discriminative approaches adapted from virtual screening face sparse, long-tailed associations and missing-not-at-random measurements: treating unrecorded pairs as negatives can suppress genuine targets. We reformulate the task as generative retrieval and introduce GenFish. Residual vector quantization converts frozen protein language model features into shared semantic identifiers. Given a molecular fingerprint, GenFish autoregressively models codes conditioned on the query and preceding code, ranking proteins by identifier likelihood without explicitly labeling unrecorded pairs as negatives. We introduce ProTargetBench, the first proteome-scale benchmark for reverse target fishing to jointly support measured-panel discrimination and full-catalogue recovery of experimentally recorded positives. Covering 20,431 UniProt-reviewed human proteins, it integrates curated bioactivity evidence and distinguishes experimental inactivity from unmeasured associations. On 198 held-out molecules, GenFish achieves higher mean performance across all three full-catalogue retrieval metrics than four discriminative neural baselines and three non-neural baselines, including ligand-based methods. A controlled positive-hiding experiment shows that targeted removal of false-negative competition improves contrastive retrieval beyond matched random masking; GenFish remains stronger under the same incomplete supervision. Pfam alignment indicates that the semantic identifiers capture biologically meaningful relationships among proteins. These results establish generative retrieval as a principled paradigm for reverse target fishing under incomplete bioactivity records.

infographic.key_insight: GenFish ranks potential protein targets for molecules using generative retrieval without explicitly treating unmeasured molecule–protein pairs as negatives.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support target discovery and drug repurposing, including oncology research, but the abstract reports no cancer-specific or clinical validation.
method: Encode frozen protein language-model features as shared semantic identifiers using residual vector quantization.
Predict identifier sequences autoregressively from a molecular fingerprint.
Rank proteins by identifier likelihood.
infographic.evidence_signal: On ProTargetBench, covering 20,431 reviewed human proteins, GenFish achieved higher mean performance across all three full-catalogue retrieval metrics than seven baselines on 198 held-out molecules.
infographic.watch_item: Recovery of recorded associations does not establish new biological targets; predictions require experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Generative Retrieval for Reverse Target Fishing with a Proteome-Scale Benchmark

title: From Adult Renal Masses to Pediatric Wilms Tumors: Evaluating Cross-Domain Generalization of Kidney Lesion Segmentation on MRI
authors: Sarah de Boer, Myrthe A. D. Buser, Hartmut Häntze, Jawed Nawabi, Lisa C. Adams, Alida F. W. van der Steeg
abstract: Deep learning segmentation models for pediatric oncology are often trained on small, single-center cohorts, whereas much larger datasets exist for adult diseases, such as kidney cancer. Whether models trained on adult renal lesions generalize to pediatric Wilms tumors remains unclear. We trained a segmentation model on single-sequence T1- or T2-weighted adult kidney MRI and evaluated it on a held-out adult test set and a pediatric Wilms tumor cohort, where it was compared with a pediatric-specific nnU-Net. Segmentation performance was quantified using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance. On the adult test set, the model achieved a median DSC of 0.86 for renal lesions. On the pediatric cohort, the adult-trained model achieved a median DSC of 0.85 compared with 0.90 for the pediatric-specific model. Despite differences in age, anatomy, and tumor type, the adult-trained model showed promising performance on pediatric Wilms tumors, with only a modest difference in median DSC compared with the pediatric-specific model. However, non-inferiority could not be shown, highlighting the value of pediatric training data. In future work, a fine-tuning strategy could be explored.

infographic.key_insight: An adult-trained kidney MRI segmentation model showed promising transfer to pediatric Wilms tumors, but non-inferiority to a pediatric-specific model was not demonstrated.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Adult MRI datasets may help develop pediatric tumor segmentation tools, although these findings concern imaging rather than cancer drug discovery.
method: Trained a segmentation model on single-sequence T1- or T2-weighted adult kidney MRI.
Evaluated it on held-out adult scans and pediatric Wilms tumor scans.
Compared pediatric performance with a pediatric-specific nnU-Net using Dice scores and 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Median lesion Dice scores were 0.86 on adult test scans and 0.85 on pediatric scans, versus 0.90 for the pediatric-specific model.
infographic.watch_item: Non-inferiority was not established, underscoring the value of pediatric training data and further validation before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: From Adult Renal Masses to Pediatric Wilms Tumors: Evaluating Cross-Domain Generalization of Kidney Lesion Segmentation on MRI

title: PRET is a few-shot system for pan-cancer recognition without example training
authors: Yi Li, Ziyu Ning, Tianqi Xiang, Qixiang Zhang, Zhihao Lin, Min Yi
abstract: Pathological examination stands as the cornerstone in cancer diagnosis, impacting millions worldwide annually. With the shortage of pathologists globally, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged rapidly to automate the diagnostics process. However, conventional AI models require substantial labeled data for each disease, posing huge challenges in scalability and practicality. Therefore, we introduce PRET (pan-cancer recognition without examples training), a few-shot system to achieve flexible, scalable, and effective cancer recognition across diverse organs, hospitals and tasks without training. Evaluated on 23 international benchmarks comprising 4,484 whole-slide images, our method outperforms existing approaches across 20 tasks, achieving over 97% area under the curve on 15 benchmarks with a maximum improvement of 36.76%. Notably, PRET delivers clinical-grade diagnostic performance in lymph node metastasis detection using only eight slide examples, outperforming 11 pathologists. By offering a flexible and cost-effective solution for pan-cancer recognition, PRET paves the way for accessible and equitable AI-based pathology systems, particularly benefiting minority populations and underserved regions.

infographic.key_insight: PRET is a few-shot AI system for pan-cancer recognition in pathology—not drug discovery—that uses a small set of examples without task-specific training.
infographic.clinical_relevance: PRET could support pathology workflows where labeled data and specialist capacity are limited, but the reported results do not establish readiness for routine clinical use.
method: Uses a few example slides for cancer recognition without task-specific training.
Targets recognition across different organs, hospitals, and tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 23 international benchmarks containing 4,484 whole-slide images, PRET reportedly outperformed existing approaches on 20 tasks and achieved over 97% AUC on 15 benchmarks; with eight example slides, it outperformed 11 pathologists in a lymph node metastasis evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Prospective clinical validation is needed to establish reliability, generalizability, and safe integration into pathology workflows.
infographic.paper_title: PRET is a few-shot system for pan-cancer recognition without example training

title: Multi-scale Fusion of Fast Vision Mamba and Foundation Model Features for Patch-Level Gleason Grading in Computational Pathology
authors: Zihe Zhang, Weimiao Yu, Piumi Don Simonge
abstract: Automated Gleason grading of prostate whole slide images (WSIs) enables faster and more consistent cancer risk stratification. However, it remains a challenging task due to the subtle morphological differences between grades, the severe class imbalance arising from rare patterns, and the diagnostic features that span multiple spatial scales. Pathology foundation models (FMs) extract strong patch representations but often operate at a single-scale, which limits spatial context and disproportionately affects classes that depend on broader context. The challenge of fusing multiple scales and complementary models, with minimal data and computational resources, remains unresolved. We propose a multi-scale classifier built on state-space models. Our method combines two complementary feature sources: a frozen foundation model, and a lightweight FastVim, pre-trained on ImageNet and distilled from the foundation model, that reads the raw image crops. At each scale, a Mamba model encodes the features from both sources with linear-time spatial context, and a jointly trained head fuses the encoded representations into one prediction. On the PANDA dataset, our method reaches macro F1 of 0.894 and Gleason 5 F1 of 0.802 under 5-fold cross-validation, a 12% and 21% relative improvement over the best single-scale model. A controlled study over 5 foundation models, 5 base classifiers and 3 scales confirms that the gain holds across encoders, with larger improvements observed at smaller scales.

infographic.key_insight: Combining multi-scale foundation-model and FastVim features improved patch-level prostate Gleason grading over the best single-scale model.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This pathology AI approach could support more consistent prostate cancer grading, but it is not a drug-discovery method or a clinically validated tool.
method: Combine frozen pathology foundation-model features with raw-image features from a lightweight, distilled FastVim.
Use Mamba state-space models to encode spatial context at each scale.
Jointly train a fusion head to produce one patch-level grade prediction.
infographic.evidence_signal: On PANDA with 5-fold cross-validation, macro F1 reached 0.894 and Gleason pattern 5 F1 reached 0.802—reported relative gains of 12% and 21% over the best single-scale model.
infographic.watch_item: External validation and slide-level clinical evaluation are needed before translating patch-level results into practice.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-scale Fusion of Fast Vision Mamba and Foundation Model Features for Patch-Level Gleason Grading in Computational Pathology

title: Multimodal-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Models for Spatiotemporal Brain MRI Forecasting
authors: Antonio Scardace, Silvia Ingala, Sebastiano Battiato, Daniele Ravì
abstract: Spatiotemporal forecasting of 3D anatomical changes is a critical generative vision challenge for modeling Alzheimer's Disease (AD) progression. While brain MRI forecasting from single-modality data has advanced, other key complementary multimodal biomarkers remain underutilized. In this work, we propose the Multimodal-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Model (MC-LDM), a novel framework for patient-specific brain MRI synthesis. MC-LDM leverages multimodal biomarkers---MRI, tau-PET, Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR), and APOE4---during training, but relies only on baseline MRI, APOE4, and patient metadata at inference, reflecting realistic clinical availability. Our contributions are threefold: (1) a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) fine-tuned via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for data-efficient learning; (2) a multimodal conditioning that integrates molecular and clinical signals to model heterogeneous disease trajectories; and (3) auxiliary predictors estimating unobserved multimodal biomarkers from MRI features and patient covariates to condition the diffusion model, removing the need for these assessments at inference. Trained on 1,355 visits from 852 subjects in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), MC-LDM reduces average regional volumetric MAE by 18% over the second-best baseline on an independent test set of 664 visits. To our knowledge, MC-LDM represents the first diffusion-based framework to leverage multimodal priors for MRI forecasting. This conceptual advancement enables patient-specific trajectory generation that captures aspects of AD heterogeneity not observable from structural anatomy alone, bridging the gap between rich multimodal supervision and the strict constraints of routine clinical deployment. Code is available at: https://github.com/antonioscardace/MC-LDM.

infographic.key_insight: MC-LDM forecasts patient-specific brain MRI changes in Alzheimer’s disease using multimodal training signals; this is not cancer drug discovery research.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support research into Alzheimer’s progression while reducing inference-time biomarker requirements, but clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Fine-tunes a latent diffusion model with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA).
Uses MRI, tau-PET, Clinical Dementia Rating, and APOE4 during training.
Predicts unavailable biomarkers from baseline MRI and patient covariates, requiring only MRI, APOE4, and metadata at inference.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained on 1,355 ADNI visits from 852 subjects, MC-LDM reduced average regional volumetric MAE by 18% versus the second-best baseline on an independent test set of 664 visits.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish generalizability beyond ADNI or whether improved volumetric accuracy translates into clinically useful individual forecasts.
infographic.paper_title: Multimodal-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Models for Spatiotemporal Brain MRI Forecasting

title: Quantifying Cancer Clinical Trial Eligibility Using Artificial Intelligence-Based Matching
authors: Goel, K. P.; Myall, N. J.; Dickerson, J.; Caswell-Jin, J. L.; Johnson, T.; Worth, J. E.; Gensheimer, M. F.
abstract: PURPOSETo develop and validate an artificial intelligence-enabled platform that combines efficient screening with explicit eligibility logic by converting unstructured cancer trial criteria into reusable structured queries, and illustrates potential eligibility using synthetic patients. METHODSWe downloaded actively recruiting US interventional treatment trials for advanced/metastatic breast cancer, colon cancer, and non-small cell lung cancer from ClinicalTrials.gov. Medical oncologists created 24 synthetic patient vignettes. A large language model converted trial eligibility criteria into Structured Query Language (SQL) code and patient information into structured records, enabling rule-based matching without further LLM inference. Cancer details and treatment history were considered, but not laboratory results or comorbidities. Validation included physician editing of generated eligibility code for 30 trials and independent assessments by two physicians, followed by consensus adjudication, for eligibility across ten trials. We descriptively summarized potential eligibility by trial characteristics and when varying age, ECOG performance status, sex, and ZIP code. RESULTSOf 833 candidate trials, 746 met inclusion criteria. Performing matching for all 746 trials took a median of 0.459 seconds per patient, excluding patient-data preparation. Against physician consensus, automated matching agreed on 230/240 patient-trial pairs (95.8%; sensitivity 83.3%, specificity 100%). Across synthetic patients, potentially eligible trials ranged from 10 to 258 without geographic restrictions. Counts decreased with worse performance status and geographic restriction and were relatively stable across ages 30-90. Later-phase, randomized, and molecularly selective trials generally matched fewer vignettes. CONCLUSIONLLM-generated SQL enables rapid, explicit rule-based screening for potential trial eligibility. Evaluation in synthetic vignettes supports feasibility, while missed matches underscore the need for further validation.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-generated SQL enabled rapid, explicit screening for potential cancer trial eligibility, with 95.8% agreement against physician consensus.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could help identify trials for clinician review, but it does not establish full eligibility or guide treatment selection.
method: Converted unstructured trial criteria into reusable SQL eligibility rules.
Structured 24 synthetic patient vignettes for rule-based matching without further LLM inference.
Screened 746 recruiting US trials for advanced breast, colon, and non-small cell lung cancers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 240 patient–trial pairs from 10 trials, agreement was 230/240, sensitivity 83.3%, and specificity 100%; screening all 746 trials took a median 0.459 seconds per patient, excluding data preparation.
infographic.watch_item: Validation used synthetic patients and omitted laboratory results and comorbidities; missed matches highlight the need for further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Quantifying Cancer Clinical Trial Eligibility Using Artificial Intelligence-Based Matching

title: What Language Adds, and at What Cost: Four Controlled Probes of Pathology Vision-Language Models
authors: Wenhao Zhang, Zhongliang Zhou, Yi Ping, Zirui Wang, Sheng Li
abstract: Vision--language models (VLMs) promise to make computational pathology queryable and able to draft reports, but how much language adds beyond the vision backbone is unclear, because almost every system is evaluated by its developers on test sets of their own choosing. We grade published evidence by how it was produced and test four claims with controlled probes that reuse released checkpoints and public data, varying one input at a time. Report text adds prognostic signal: adding a frozen embedding of the stage-redacted report to a slide embedding raises the pooled C-index by 0.019 for progression-free interval and by 0.016 for overall survival across 1{,}633 TCGA patients, and restoring the stage statement adds nothing. Prompts add no measurable accuracy at inference: with features and pooling fixed, zero-shot classification is statistically indistinguishable from a supervised linear probe for lung and renal cancer subtyping. Slide-level question answering is barely grounded: SlideChat answers 74.82\% of SlideBench-VQA(TCGA) items correctly with the slide and 74.41\% without it, whereas its language backbone alone reaches 43.52\%. Paraphrasing leaves accuracy unchanged but flips 8--23\% of answers. Self-reported gains from agentic navigation and few-shot language priors cannot yet be attributed to language. Language thus adds real but narrow value, and we propose minimum controls that would expose these failure modes in future evaluations.

infographic.key_insight: Language added modest prognostic value to pathology slide features, but prompts did not measurably improve classification and slide-level question answering showed little dependence on images.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These findings inform evaluation of pathology AI for cancer prognosis and reporting, not drug discovery or treatment selection.
method: Used released checkpoints and public data in four controlled probes.
Compared slide-only prognosis with added stage-redacted report embeddings.
Tested classification prompts, image removal, and question paraphrasing.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 1,633 TCGA patients, report embeddings increased pooled C-index by 0.019 for progression-free interval and 0.016 for overall survival; SlideChat accuracy was 74.82% with slides versus 74.41% without.
infographic.watch_item: Clinical utility remains unestablished, and gains attributed to agentic navigation or few-shot language priors lack sufficient controls to isolate language's contribution.
infographic.paper_title: What Language Adds, and at What Cost: Four Controlled Probes of Pathology Vision-Language Models

title: MCDA: Multi-View Graph Contrastive Learning with Dynamic Topology Augmentation for Functional MRI Analysis
authors: Hao Zhang, Xiaoyun Liu, Shuo Huang, Yue Ma, Liang Cao, Mingxia Liu
abstract: Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) is a vital non-invasive tool for diagnosing brain disorders and uncovering pathological mechanisms. However, existing graph contrastive learning (GCL) methods often underexploit augmentation histories across training epochs and the relationships among different augmented views. In this paper, we introduce a topology-guided Multi-view graph Contrastive learning framework with Dynamic graph topology Augmentation (MCDA) for fMRI analysis. Unlike traditional GCL that uses fixed noise or edge-dropping, MCDA employs a Dynamic Augmentation Update (DAU) module that iteratively refines the augmented topology. Specifically, we incorporate self-aware and cross-sample augmentation strategies to simultaneously capture individual-specific functional signatures and inter-subject heterogeneity. We then design a topology-guided multi-view graph contrastive learning scheme that explores interrelationships not only between the original network and its augmented views, but also across different augmented views to maximize structural information preservation. We characterize the score-level optimization directions and establish a lower bound for the contrastive objective. The framework combines classification and contrastive losses for brain disorder diagnosis and examines discriminative functional connectivity patterns as potential biomarkers. Experiments on two public rs-fMRI datasets comprising 1,236 subjects demonstrate that MCDA outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. The code has been made publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/goodcodingagoodboy/MCDA}.

infographic.key_insight: MCDA dynamically refines brain-network augmentations and learns relationships across multiple graph views to improve rs-fMRI-based brain disorder classification, rather than cancer drug discovery.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework may support research into brain disorder classification and candidate functional-connectivity biomarkers, but clinical utility is not established.
method: Iteratively update graph topology using a Dynamic Augmentation Update module.
Combine self-aware and cross-sample augmentation to capture individual signatures and inter-subject differences.
Jointly optimize classification and topology-guided contrastive losses across original and augmented graphs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports outperforming state-of-the-art methods on two public rs-fMRI datasets totaling 1,236 subjects, without providing numerical performance estimates.
infographic.watch_item: Generalizability to independent clinical populations and robustness across imaging sites remain unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: MCDA: Multi-View Graph Contrastive Learning with Dynamic Topology Augmentation for Functional MRI Analysis

title: Arbitrary-Scale Anisotropic 3D MRI Super-Resolution with Gaussian Prototypes
authors: Aditya Rastogi, Ramon Leiser, Prateek Singh, Martha Foltyn-Dumitru, Martin Bendszus, Fabian Bamberg
abstract: Reducing MRI acquisition time improves patient comfort, reduces motion artefacts, and increases scanner throughput. Clinical protocols often shorten acquisitions by sacrificing spatial resolution, particularly along the slice axis. Super-resolution can recover higher-resolution images, but existing methods are typically specialised to one scale or acquisition geometry, limiting their use across heterogeneous clinical protocols. We present GSMR3D, a continuous volumetric model that reconstructs arbitrary isotropic and anisotropic resolutions with a single checkpoint per MRI contrast. It combines a learned dictionary of anisotropic 3D Gaussian prototypes with scale-conditioned frequency encoding and an exact measurement-consistency projection, keeping reconstructions consistent with the acquired low-resolution data. We train separate models on 3,731 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted and 30,254 T1-weighted brain MRI volumes from clinical and population-based cohorts. We evaluate GSMR3D against geometry-specific specialists for isotropic, in-plane, and through-plane super-resolution using reconstruction quality and downstream tasks: brain tumour segmentation, brain-metastasis detection, and brain parcellation. GSMR3D outperforms specialists at isotropic $2\times$ and achieves better LPIPS, DISTS, and FID across all geometries, although specialists retain higher PSNR in anisotropic settings. It more faithfully preserves glioma segmentations across all geometries, achieves the highest lesion sensitivity on an independent brain-metastasis cohort, and the highest brain-parcellation agreement for isotropic and in-plane reconstruction. Reconstruction takes about 6s per volume, adding little overhead relative to acquisition-time savings. GSMR3D offers a flexible approach to MRI scan-time reduction with one model per contrast across geometries while preserving information relevant to downstream tasks.

infographic.key_insight: GSMR3D uses one model per MRI contrast to reconstruct varied 3D resolutions, preserving tumour-relevant information without separate models for each acquisition geometry.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support shorter brain MRI acquisitions while retaining information useful for tumour segmentation and metastasis detection; it is imaging research, not cancer drug discovery.
method: Represents MRI volumes with learned anisotropic 3D Gaussian prototypes.
Uses scale-conditioned frequency encoding for arbitrary isotropic and anisotropic reconstruction.
Applies an exact measurement-consistency projection to match acquired low-resolution data.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained on 3,731 contrast-enhanced T1 and 30,254 T1 brain MRI volumes, GSMR3D improved perceptual metrics across evaluated geometries and achieved the highest lesion sensitivity on an independent brain-metastasis cohort.
infographic.watch_item: Specialist models retained higher PSNR in anisotropic settings, and downstream task results do not establish prospective clinical benefit.
infographic.paper_title: Arbitrary-Scale Anisotropic 3D MRI Super-Resolution with Gaussian Prototypes

title: DR-Learners for Generalizing CATEs from a Randomized Controlled Trial
authors: Vanessa Rodriguez, Brieuc Lehmann, Karla Diaz-Ordaz
abstract: Randomized clinical trials are essential for evaluating interventions, yet average treatment effects can obscure treatment effect heterogeneity, making conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) a natural target. However, restrictive eligibility criteria and differential trial participation can limit the generalizability of these effects to broader target populations. Building on existing DR-Learners, we develop the gDR-Learner for generalizing RCT CATEs to a target population, using cross-fitted machine-learning nuisance estimation. We derive excess-risk bounds in which nuisance errors enter only as products, showing that the estimator achieves oracle-rate convergence despite slower individual nuisance estimation. The variables needed to generalize are rarely measured across the entire target population. We therefore extend the methods to two settings with incomplete covariate information: when certain covariates are measured only in the trial (e.g., biomarkers), and covariates driving trial participation measured only in a subsample of the target population, such as a representative cohort or registry. We construct weighted conformal prediction intervals for individual treatment effects, accounting for covariate shift between the trial and target population. In simulations, the gDR-Learner achieved the lowest estimation error when all covariates were observed relative to standard T- and DR-Learners and an inverse-probability-weighted T-Learner, and also outperformed the latter under incomplete covariate observation. We illustrate the methods by reanalyzing the Coronary Artery Surgery Study, examining treatment effect heterogeneity by prior myocardial infarction and baseline ejection fraction.

infographic.key_insight: The gDR-Learner estimates how treatment effects vary across a target population beyond a randomized trial, including settings with incomplete covariate data.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This statistical methods study could help assess treatment-effect heterogeneity beyond trial participants; it is not an AI cancer drug discovery study.
method: Combines cross-fitted machine learning with doubly robust estimation to generalize conditional average treatment effects.
Extends estimation to covariates observed only in the trial or a target-population subsample.
Constructs weighted conformal intervals for individual treatment effects under covariate shift.
infographic.evidence_signal: In simulations, gDR-Learner had the lowest estimation error among tested methods with complete covariates and outperformed the weighted T-Learner with incomplete covariates; an application reanalyzed the Coronary Artery Surgery Study.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization depends on the assumptions needed to link trial and target populations; incomplete covariates remain an implementation challenge.
infographic.paper_title: DR-Learners for Generalizing CATEs from a Randomized Controlled Trial

title: On the Selectivity of Generative Models in Structure-Based Drug Design
authors: Ella Miray Rajaonson, Jungyoon Lee, William Chau, Alan Aspuru-Guzik, Benjamin Sanchez-Lengeling, Dominique Beaini
abstract: Designing small-molecule drugs that selectively bind to a target protein while avoiding unintended interactions with other proteins is essential for reducing side effects that contribute substantially to clinical attrition. Although structure-based drug design (SBDD) has advanced rapidly with deep learning, most generative models still optimize binding to a single target and disregard selectivity due to limited training data and unknown off-target interactions. Motivated by this gap, we introduce SELECTBENCH, a comprehensive benchmark assessing the selectivity of generative SBDD models. SELECTBENCH provides three curated evaluation tasks reflecting different real-world drug discovery scenarios: literature-based case studies, safety screening panels used in pharmaceutical development, and large-scale structure-based evaluation sets. We further introduce a suite of metrics to quantify selectivity and conduct a systematic evaluation of nine representative SBDD models, including methods explicitly trained for selectivity and widely-used inference-time guidance techniques. Our results show that even selectivity-trained models achieve only modest off-target discrimination and inference-time guidance provides limited gains, underscoring the need for method improvement. SELECTBENCH provides both a characterization of where current generative SBDD stands on selectivity and an open, extensible platform to accelerate progress. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/lovetaro/selectbench.

infographic.key_insight: SELECTBENCH shows that current generative structure-based drug design models offer only modest discrimination between target and off-target proteins.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Better molecular selectivity could support safer drug discovery, including oncology, but this study does not establish clinical safety or cancer-specific benefit.
method: Introduce SELECTBENCH to evaluate molecular selectivity.
Assess literature cases, pharmaceutical safety panels, and large-scale protein-structure sets.
Compare nine models, including selectivity-trained methods and inference-time guidance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three evaluation tasks, selectivity-trained models showed modest off-target discrimination, while inference-time guidance provided limited gains.
infographic.watch_item: Computational selectivity results require experimental validation and cannot rule out unknown off-target interactions.
infographic.paper_title: On the Selectivity of Generative Models in Structure-Based Drug Design

title: PRISM: Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling to Enhance Solubility OOD Generalization
authors: Xinyi Chen, Jiahuan Pang, Titus Chima, Paul Weng, Wendong Wang
abstract: Solubility depends on intermolecular interactions between solutes and solvents, and is central to drug discovery, chemical and materials process engineering. Its prediction requires out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization to unseen solutes, solvents, and solvent mixtures, where supervised methods suffer from data scarcity, and existing self-supervised methods do not explicitly learn chemically meaningful relations. Learning chemically meaningful relational information without labels can alleviate data scarcity and improve OOD generalization, but remains challenging. We introduce Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling (PRISM) and apply it to solubility OOD generalization. PRISM is a label-free pretraining framework that converts expert-defined chemical priors into relational teachers. For solubility prediction, it trains four encoders to preserve the population-level relational information from priors capturing hydrophobic, electrostatic, polarizability, and substructural effects, using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence to match distance-based neighborhood distributions during pretraining. Across scaffold, solute, and solvent OOD settings, PRISM matches or surpasses supervised and self-supervised baselines. Under mixed-solvent OOD, freezing the four PRISM encoders and training a lightweight fusion-and-composition head outperforms strong baselines and substantially reduces run-to-run variation. Ablations and control studies confirm that gains stem from chemically meaningful relational structures baked into the encoders by PRISM. We expect this strategy of turning relational priors into self-supervision signals to extend beyond solubility prediction to domains where chemically or biologically meaningful relational priors are available.

infographic.key_insight: PRISM uses chemical priors as label-free learning signals to improve solubility prediction for unseen compounds, solvents, and solvent mixtures.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Better solubility prediction could support drug discovery, including oncology programs, but this study does not establish cancer-specific or clinical benefits.
method: Convert hydrophobic, electrostatic, polarizability, and substructural priors into relational teachers.
Pretrain four encoders by matching distance-based neighborhood distributions using KL divergence.
For mixed-solvent prediction, freeze the encoders and train a lightweight fusion-and-composition head.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across scaffold, solute, and solvent out-of-distribution evaluations, PRISM matched or surpassed baselines; mixed-solvent tests showed stronger performance and lower run-to-run variation, with ablations supporting the contribution of chemical relations.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no dataset sizes or numerical effect estimates, limiting assessment of improvement magnitude and practical generalizability.
infographic.paper_title: PRISM: Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling to Enhance Solubility OOD Generalization

title: Progressive multi-scale tumor-state memory for incomplete multimodal brain tumor segmentation
authors: Milad Rostamian, Mohammadreza Mohammadi, Mohsen Soryani
abstract: Brain tumor segmentation uses complementary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sequences, but some sequences may be unavailable in practice. Their absence changes the information available for segmenting different tumor regions. Fusion methods can support different input subsets. However, fusion at several scales does not by itself specify how tumor evidence is retained and updated to guide fusion at later stages. We propose a progressive multi-scale tumor-state memory network (PMTM) for segmentation from any non-empty subset of T1ce, T1, FLAIR, and T2. PMTM maintains a compact state for the current subject across the encoder stages. At each stage, we use assignment maps to pool spatial features into ordered evidence vectors for each available modality. We average these vectors across the available modalities, and a learned gate combines this evidence with the previous state. The up- dated state guides residual fusion at that stage and is used in the state update at the next stage. A modality-token mixer also models interactions among the available modalities at each stage. We apply semantic supervision to the assignment maps at all four stages. We evaluate PMTM on BraTS2018, BraTS2020, and BraTS2023 GLI across all 15 non-empty modality subsets. Averaged over the three tumor regions and the 15 subsets, PMTM achieves Dice scores of 75.31%, 77.54%, and 80.47% on BraTS2018, BraTS2020, and BraTS2023 GLI, respectively. These scores are higher than those of RobustSeg, RFNet, and mmFormer in our experiments on each dataset. Component ablations and internal state analysis are performed on BraTS2020.

infographic.key_insight: PMTM retains and updates tumor evidence across imaging scales to segment brain tumors when one or more MRI sequences are unavailable.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This imaging study—not a drug discovery study—could support tumor delineation with incomplete MRI inputs, but clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Accepts any non-empty subset of T1ce, T1, FLAIR, and T2 MRI.
Pools modality evidence into a compact subject-specific memory, updated through a learned gate across encoder stages.
Uses memory-guided residual fusion, modality-token mixing, and semantic supervision at four stages.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across all 15 non-empty modality subsets and three tumor regions, mean Dice scores were 75.31%, 77.54%, and 80.47% on BraTS2018, BraTS2020, and BraTS2023 GLI, respectively, exceeding RobustSeg, RFNet, and mmFormer in the reported experiments.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark results do not establish prospective clinical performance or robustness to real-world MRI acquisition differences.
infographic.paper_title: Progressive multi-scale tumor-state memory for incomplete multimodal brain tumor segmentation

title: Localization Gains from Explanation Regularization Should Not Be Interpreted as Faithfulness Gains.
authors: Amrin Akter, Mauro Dalla Mura, Diana Mateus, Dawood Al Chanti
abstract: Training-time explanation regularization is often evaluated by whether saliency maps become more concentrated within annotated regions. We argue that this criterion alone is insufficient: transformation consistency, lesion localization, and faithfulness to the classifier are distinct properties and should be evaluated separately, particularly in medical imaging. We examine this distinction through a case study of Contrastive Grad-CAM Consistency (CGC) in three-class brain tumor MRI classification. Using a single-channel ResNet-50 with five-fold patient-grouped cross-validation, we compare a cross-entropy baseline with CGC. CGC changes overall Pointing Game (PG) from $27.24\%$ to $36.02\%$ and Relevance Mass Accuracy (RMA) from $11.17\%$ to $18.01\%$, while classification accuracy changes from $93.63\%$ to $94.87\%$. Perturbation-based faithfulness metrics show inconsistent changes: Insertion Area Under the Curve (IAUC) changes from $0.73$ to $0.78$, whereas Deletion Area Under the Curve (DAUC) favors the baseline ($0.36$ versus $0.41$; lower is better), and overall Iterative Removal Of Features (IROF) is $0.57$ for both models. These results support our position that improved spatial agreement with pathology should not be interpreted as a general improvement in explanation faithfulness. We therefore recommend property-specific evaluation in which the property targeted by the explanation objective, spatial agreement with reference regions, and model reliance are measured and reported separately.

infographic.key_insight: More tumor-focused saliency maps do not necessarily explain a classifier’s decisions more faithfully.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For brain tumor MRI AI, better visual alignment with lesions should not be treated as evidence of more reliable explanations or clinical readiness.
method: Compared cross-entropy training with Contrastive Grad-CAM Consistency regularization.
Used a single-channel ResNet-50 for three-class brain tumor MRI classification.
Evaluated localization, classification accuracy, and perturbation-based faithfulness separately.
infographic.evidence_signal: In five-fold patient-grouped cross-validation, localization improved (PG: 27.24% to 36.02%; RMA: 11.17% to 18.01%), but faithfulness was mixed: insertion improved, deletion worsened, and IROF was unchanged.
infographic.watch_item: This imaging case study does not establish generalizability, clinical benefit, or relevance to cancer drug discovery.
infographic.paper_title: Localization Gains from Explanation Regularization Should Not Be Interpreted as Faithfulness Gains.

title: Pathology foundation models for training-free case retrieval in salivary gland tumors
authors: Maximilian J. Roesel, Niklas Kiermeyer, Philipp Keyl, Frederick Klauschen
abstract: In pathology, pattern recognition relies on a frame of reference built through extensive training and experience, which may still fall short when encountering rare cancer subtypes. Archives of previously diagnosed tumors often contain relevant precedents, yet identifying the most relevant cases remains challenging. Here we explore whether content-based retrieval with current pathology foundation models facilitates rare cancer diagnostics without any task-specific training. Pathologists can query a digitized archive using a region of interest (ROI) from a whole slide image (WSI) and retrieve morphologically similar cases, along with their ICD-O codes and corresponding WSIs. The ROI can be selected manually or automatically using a gated attention-based multiple instance learning model. We evaluate our approach by leave-one-case-out on an imbalanced dataset of 137 salivary gland tumor cases spanning 12 ICD-O morphology categories, comparing four pathology foundation models (Atlas2, Atlas2-B, Atlas2-S, and UNI2h). Top-1/3/5 retrieval was 62.5%/76.7%/81.3% for Atlas2, 50.2/66.6/72.9% for UNI2h, 52.3%/71.5%/77.6% for Atlas2-B and 54.4/65.2/73.7% for Atlas2-S. Macro-averaged F1 ranged from 69.0% for the smallest model Atlas2-S to 76.6% for the largest model Atlas2 across the five classes with at least ten cases. Our modified Chamfer similarity separated correct from incorrect matches among the Top-5 more reliably for Atlas2 (AUC 0.754) than for Atlas2-B (0.679, p = 0.020) and Atlas2-S (0.653, p = 0.003), but not UNI2h (0.697, p = 0.196). Requiring no additional training or manual annotation, this approach makes departmental archives searchable with pathology foundation models, providing a low-barrier route to case-based differential diagnosis and extending the individual frame of reference to the collective experience of the department.

infographic.key_insight: Pathology foundation models enabled training-free retrieval of similar salivary gland tumor cases, with Atlas2 achieving the highest reported Top-1/3/5 retrieval performance.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Retrieving archived cases and their diagnostic codes could support case-based differential diagnosis of rare tumors, though this study did not evaluate clinical diagnostic benefit or drug discovery.
method: Query a digitized archive with a manually or automatically selected whole-slide image region.
Retrieve morphologically similar cases, ICD-O codes, and corresponding slides without task-specific retrieval training.
Compare Atlas2, Atlas2-B, Atlas2-S, and UNI2h using leave-one-case-out evaluation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 137 cases across 12 ICD-O categories, Atlas2 achieved 62.5%, 76.7%, and 81.3% Top-1/3/5 retrieval; macro-F1 was assessed only for the five classes with at least 10 cases.
infographic.watch_item: The small, imbalanced dataset limits generalizability; broader external validation is needed before routine diagnostic use.
infographic.paper_title: Pathology foundation models for training-free case retrieval in salivary gland tumors

title: How Robust Are Prognostic Radiomic Features? Comparing Selection Techniques on Pooled Glioblastoma Cohorts
authors: Yannick Sodonougbo, Marlene Schnieders, Alexia Rizoudis, Santiago Cepeda, Frank Kramer, Dominik Müller
abstract: Radiomic survival studies in glioblastoma report heterogeneous prognostic features, but how much of this stems from the methodology itself is rarely examined. We analysed the association of 463 radiomic, anatomical and clinical features from pre-treatment MRI with overall survival in 705 IDH-wildtype glioblastoma patients from three public cohorts, using three techniques: a log-rank test after median split, univariate Cox regression (both Benjamini-Hochberg corrected) and an XGBoost regressor interpreted with SHAP. The log-rank test selected 99 features, Cox regression 72 and SHAP its top 20; five were selected by all three: age, a peritumoural T2 texture feature, the number of connected peritumoural mask components and two image-level intensity maxima. The two survival tests shared 51 features, about half of the SHAP top 20 were also selected by either test, and where selections overlapped, effect directions agreed. Many selections were PyRadiomics diagnostic descriptors that are not restricted to tumour voxels. Analytical pipeline choices, including ranking method, pre-filtering and descriptor handling, can substantially influence which features appear prognostic.

infographic.key_insight: Feature-selection methods identified markedly different prognostic features in glioblastoma, with only five shared across all three approaches.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The findings highlight robustness concerns for MRI-based survival biomarkers in glioblastoma, rather than establishing tools for treatment selection or drug discovery.
method: Analysed 463 MRI-derived radiomic, anatomical and clinical features for association with overall survival.
Compared median-split log-rank tests and univariate Cox regression, both Benjamini–Hochberg corrected.
Compared statistical selections with the top 20 features from an XGBoost regressor interpreted using SHAP.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 705 IDH-wildtype glioblastoma patients from three public cohorts, log-rank and Cox analyses selected 99 and 72 features respectively, sharing 51; overlapping selections agreed in effect direction.
infographic.watch_item: Many selected features were diagnostic descriptors not restricted to tumour voxels, making descriptor handling and analytical pipeline choices important interpretation concerns.
infographic.paper_title: How Robust Are Prognostic Radiomic Features? Comparing Selection Techniques on Pooled Glioblastoma Cohorts

title: GraphBEAT: Graph-based Bucketized Event Aggregation Over Time for Early Risk Stratification of Gastrointestinal Cancers
authors: Leo Y. Li-Han, Chris Varghese, Elizabeth B. Habermann, Mark J. Truty, William R. G. Perry, Cornelius A. Thiels
abstract: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) contain complementary diagnostic and laboratory information about patient health. However, irregularity, sparsity, heterogeneity, and incompleteness in documentation complicate EHR modeling. To address the problem, we introduce GraphBEAT (Graph-based Bucketized Event Aggregation over Time), a temporal graph representation learning framework that groups clinical events into time buckets and transforms observed features into patient-specific, temporally directed graphs to enable early risk stratification for gastrointestinal cancers. Each node in an EHR graph encodes feature identity, observed value, and temporal position of clinical events. A context-aware, time-decay message-passing mechanism models transitions between successive buckets, followed by multi-head attention pooling to generate patient-level representations. GraphBEAT was trained and evaluated on multi-site longitudinal diagnosis codes and laboratory tests to predict pancreatic, liver, and intestinal cancer at 12-, 24-, and 36-month diagnostic lead times. In all experimental setups, GraphBEAT consistently outperformed baseline graph neural networks (GraphSAGE, GAT, and GCN) and sequence modeling approaches (Transformer and long short-term memory [LSTM]). GraphBEAT also required over 250x fewer floating-point operations per patient and over 20x fewer parameters than the Transformer and LSTM baselines. These results support GraphBEAT as an accurate and computationally efficient approach for cancer risk stratification from sparse, heterogeneous longitudinal health records.

infographic.key_insight: GraphBEAT outperformed tested graph and sequence models for gastrointestinal cancer risk stratification while using substantially fewer computational resources.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support earlier identification of pancreatic, liver, and intestinal cancer risk from longitudinal health records; it is not a drug discovery method.
method: Groups diagnosis and laboratory events into time buckets to build patient-specific, temporally directed graphs.
Encodes event identity, observed value, and temporal position in graph nodes.
Combines context-aware, time-decay message passing with multi-head attention pooling.
infographic.evidence_signal: In multi-site EHR evaluations at 12-, 24-, and 36-month diagnostic lead times, GraphBEAT outperformed all tested baselines and required over 250× fewer operations per patient and over 20× fewer parameters than Transformer and LSTM models.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report absolute predictive performance, calibration, or prospective clinical validation, leaving real-world utility uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: GraphBEAT: Graph-based Bucketized Event Aggregation Over Time for Early Risk Stratification of Gastrointestinal Cancers

title: Dirichlet-Tree Allocation Priors for Bayesian Causal Forests
authors: Javier Enrique Aguilar, Daniel Klippert, Yusufhan Balci, Alexander Marx
abstract: Bayesian Causal Forests (BCF) estimate heterogeneous treatment effects with a separate ensemble of treatment trees. The prior on the leaf values of the treatment trees determines whether sampling variability is attributed to the treatment effect. Independent shrinkage priors exert no control over how a tree allocates variability across its leaves, and their total prior variance grows as leaves are added. We propose the Dirichlet-Tree Bayesian Causal Forest, which jointly regularizes the leaf values of each treatment tree through a Dirichlet-Tree prior on their variance shares, generated by stick-breaking along the tree topology. We characterize the spike and tails of the marginal leaf prior, show that the prior adaptively bounds the number of regions of effect heterogeneity, and establish posterior consistency for the forest. In simulations, the model outperforms BCF when heterogeneity is confined to a few regions and reduces spurious heterogeneity elsewhere, and, unlike independent shrinkage priors, its accuracy does not deteriorate as the trees grow. We also evaluate the model on real data, including a pancreatic cancer survival study.

infographic.key_insight: A Dirichlet-Tree prior helps Bayesian Causal Forests concentrate treatment-effect heterogeneity in a few regions while reducing spurious variation elsewhere.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The method could support research into heterogeneous treatment effects in oncology, but the abstract does not establish clinical utility or drug discovery performance.
method: Jointly regularizes treatment-tree leaf values using prior variance shares.
Allocates variance through stick-breaking along the tree topology.
Adaptively bounds heterogeneity regions and establishes posterior consistency.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations showed improvements over standard BCF when heterogeneity was localized, with accuracy maintained as trees grew; real-data evaluations included a pancreatic cancer survival study.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative oncology results, and causal interpretation depends on appropriate study-design and identification assumptions.
infographic.paper_title: Dirichlet-Tree Allocation Priors for Bayesian Causal Forests

title: Label-Space Mismatch Distorts Cross-Cohort Evaluation in Breast Cancer Molecular Subtyping
authors: Suxing Liu, Byungwon Min, Zhijian Zheng, Jiahao Wang
abstract: Cross-cohort evaluation of breast cancer subtype classifiers is unreliable when source and target cohorts use different annotation standards: METABRIC labels six classes, PAM50 defines five, and a claudin-low prediction cannot be correct under a five-class standard. A classifier transferred from 1,369 METABRIC patients (train n=958) to TCGA-BRCA (n=987) and GSE21653 (n=266) separates three evaluation operations routinely conflated in cross-site comparisons. (1) Label-space restriction - an evaluation-rule change, not a retraining gain - is the dominant correction (73.76%->79.74% on TCGA-BRCA; 63.16%->68.42% on GSE21653); (2) EM prior correction on the reconciled space is an optional calibration step (Brier fidelity up, macro F1 down; to 80.65% and 74.06%); and (3) the target label space is not recoverable from unlabelled predictions (EM retains prior 0.0751 on the absent class; calibrated detectors fail), so compliance must come from cohort documentation. The protocol exposes why internal validation overstates cross-cohort value: multimodal fusion gains do not transfer (no configuration beats mRNA alone, n=694; McNemar p=0.13-1.00), and the genomic panel adds nothing to pathological complete response prediction over clinical variables (DeltaAUC = +0.0045). Clinically, without label-space compliance, cross-site accuracy comparisons misattribute annotation-standard differences to model skill; Luminal A/B and claudin-low boundary errors map to distinct treatment decisions; and subtype accuracy is a weaker portable endpoint than survival discrimination (external C-index 0.577-0.584). Reporting the cohort's allowed label set and applying label-space compliance are therefore prerequisites before any cross-cohort performance claim.

infographic.key_insight: Cross-cohort breast cancer subtype accuracy is distorted by incompatible label sets, making label-space alignment essential before attributing performance differences to model skill.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Reliable subtype evaluation matters because subtype boundaries can affect treatment interpretation, but this study does not establish improved treatment outcomes.
method: Transfer a METABRIC-trained subtype classifier to TCGA-BRCA and GSE21653.
Separate label-space restriction from optional EM prior calibration.
Evaluate multimodal transfer, response prediction, and survival discrimination.
infographic.evidence_signal: Restricting predictions to each target cohort’s allowed labels raised accuracy from 73.76% to 79.74% in TCGA-BRCA (n=987) and from 63.16% to 68.42% in GSE21653 (n=266), without retraining.
infographic.watch_item: Allowed labels must come from cohort documentation, not unlabelled predictions; optional EM calibration improved Brier performance but reduced macro F1.
infographic.paper_title: Label-Space Mismatch Distorts Cross-Cohort Evaluation in Breast Cancer Molecular Subtyping
